papers.title: A Multicenter 13-Week Evaluation of the twiist Automated Insulin Delivery in Insulin-Treated Type 2 Diabetes: The twiist-T2D Pivotal Trial.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the efficacy, safety, and user satisfaction of the twiist automated insulin delivery (AID) system in adults with type 2 diabetes. In a single-arm, multicenter trial, 307 adults with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, 19-85 years old, initiated use of the twiist AID system for 13 weeks after collection of baseline continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data. The primary outcome was change in HbA1c from baseline to 13 weeks. Mean HbA1c decreased by 0.7% (95% CI -0.9 to -0.6) from 8.1% ± 1.5% at baseline to 7.4% ± 0.9% after using twiist for 13 weeks (P < 0.001 for both noninferiority and superiority). The treatment effect was greatest in participants with baseline HbA1c ≥9.0%. A substantial HbA1c reduction was observed when AID was added to prestudy use of a glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist or sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor drug, which was continued during the trial. Mean CGM-measured time-in-range 70-180 mg/dL increased from 57% ± 26% to 73% ± 17% (mean change 16% [95% CI 14-18]; P < 0.001). All other multiplicity-controlled CGM outcomes reflective of hyperglycemia showed significant improvement from baseline. The frequency of CGM-measured hypoglycemia was low at baseline and remained low during follow-up. Diabetic ketoacidosis occurred in one participant; no severe hypoglycemia events occurred. Using twiist, participant satisfaction was higher than with their prestudy insulin delivery method (P < 0.001) and sleep quality improved (P < 0.001). In this single-arm, 13-week trial in adults with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, AID with the twiist system was safe and associated with substantially improved glycemia.

papers.title: In Response to DISE and Rhinomanometry Correlates of Response to Head-Of-Bed Elevation in Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
In Reference to DISE and Rhinomanometry Correlates of Response to Head-Of-Bed Elevation in Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
Association between varicose veins and central serous chorioretinopathy.
papers.abstract: AimTo investigate the association between varicose veins and central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR), based on emerging genetic evidence of a shared vascular mechanism. Propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Patients with varicose veins (n=621 513) were matched 1:1 to controls without varicose veins on age, sex, race and ethnicity, with prior CSCR or serous pigment epithelial detachment (PED) excluded. A secondary analysis excluded glucocorticoid users and additionally matched on hypertension, sleep apnoea and healthcare utilisation. A tertiary analysis compared thromboembolic risk (pulmonary embolism (PE) and deep vein thrombosis (DVT)) in varicose vein patients with and without CSCR. Varicose veins were significantly associated with CSCR (risk ratio (RR) 2.16; 95% CI 1.86 to 2.52; p<0.0001) and serous PED (RR 1.97; 95% CI 1.69 to 2.93; p<0.0001). Associations persisted after excluding glucocorticoid users and adjusting for comorbidities (CSCR RR 1.83; 95% CI 1.22 to 2.75; p=0.003; PED RR 1.95; 95% CI 1.38 to 3.34; p=0.013). Among varicose vein patients, rates of DVT (RR 1.36; p=0.078) and PE (RR 1.41; p=0.14) did not differ significantly between those with and without CSCR. Varicose veins were significantly associated with CSCR and serous PED, independent of glucocorticoid exposure and known comorbidities, supporting a possible systemic vascular mechanism in CSCR pathophysiology.

papers.title: Early interventions for primary care patients with stress-related mental ill health: a randomised controlled non-inferiority trial of a nurse-led collaborative care intervention versus cognitive behavioural therapy.
papers.abstract: Stress-related mental ill health is highly prevalent, and most individuals first seek help in primary care where access to psychological support is often limited. To test whether nurse-led collaborative care (CC) is non-inferior to cognitive behavioural therapy delivered as psychologist-guided self-help (GSH-CBT) in reducing stress for adult primary care patients with stress-related mental ill health. A randomised controlled non-inferiority trial where 172 adult primary care patients with mild to moderate stress-related mental ill health were allocated to nurse-led CC or GSH-CBT (1:1). The primary outcome was the Perceived Stress Scale-10 administered every 3 weeks during the 12-week treatment phase. The a priori non-inferiority margin was 0.3 d, requiring the one-sided 95% CI of the effect size to fall within this bound. Secondary outcomes were symptoms of exhaustion, sleep problems, depressive symptoms, general anxiety and quality of life. In both conditions, participants showed large, significant within-group improvements on the primary outcome and all secondary outcomes. The primary outcome showed a small between-group difference (d=0.22), favouring GSH-CBT, with the CI upper bound (0.52) exceeding the non-inferiority margin. For secondary outcomes, GSH-CBT led to a greater reduction in exhaustion (d=0.28; 95% CI 0.64 to 0.002). No other between-group differences were observed. Nurse-led CC was not non-inferior to GSH-CBT. Effect differences were small, but improvements were slightly larger in GSH-CBT. Given that nurse-led CC is safe, easy to administer, and that significant within-group improvements were observed across all measures, this intervention could be a viable option in primary care settings where psychologist-delivered treatment is limited.

papers.title: Trajectory changes in psychosocial adaptation levels of patients after implantation of cardiac implantable electronic devices and development of the intervention programme: a mixed-methods research protocol.
papers.abstract: The implantation of cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) has become an important treatment for various types of arrhythmias and severe heart failure, effectively improving patient prognosis and increasing survival rates. However, patients after CIED implantation need to go through a process of coexisting with and adapting to the internal electronic device. This may result in limitations in daily activities, discomfort and lifestyle changes, which can easily lead to negative emotions and psychosocial maladjustment in the patients, seriously affecting their physical and mental rehabilitation and prognosis. This study aims to explore the trajectory of psychosocial adaptation and its influencing factors among patients after CIED implantation and to gain an in-depth understanding of their process of physical and psychological adjustment. Drawing on the research findings and existing literature, this study will develop an intervention programme to improve psychosocial adaptation among patients after CIED implantation, thereby providing a theoretical and practical basis for future clinical interventions in this population. This study focuses on patients who have undergone CIED implantation. A mixed-methods approach will be adopted, combining a cross-sectional survey, a prospective longitudinal quantitative design and a qualitative design. (1) Quantitative study: The Basic Information Questionnaire, Chinese version of Self-report Psychosocial Adjustment to Illness Scale, Chinese version of Medical Coping Modes Questionnaire, Chinese version of Acceptance of Illness Scale, Chinese version of Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support, Self-efficacy for Managing Chronic Disease and Health Literacy Management Scale will be administered to patients after CIED implantation to explore the latent categories, associated factors and longitudinal trajectories of psychosocial adaptation. Statistical analysis will be conducted using Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 26 (SPSS 26) and Mplus software. (2) Qualitative study: Based on descriptive phenomenology, semi-structured interviews will be conducted with patients after CIED implantation to gain an in-depth understanding of their life experiences of psychosocial adaptation, as well as their process of physical and psychological adjustment. The data will be analysed using the Colaizzi 7-step method of phenomenological analysis, supported by NVivo software for data organisation and coding. (3) Development of the intervention programme: Based on the literature review and theoretical framework, and integrating findings from both the quantitative and qualitative phases, an intervention programme for improving the psychosocial adaptation among patients after CIED implantation will be initially developed. The Delphi method will be used to evaluate and revise the initially developed intervention programme. A pilot test will subsequently be conducted to further refine the programme. This research plan has been approved by the Ethics Committee of the First People's Hospital of Foshan (Approval Number: LSY-2025-019). Data collection is authorised by the Ethics Committee of the First People's Hospital of Foshan. The results of this study will be published in relevant peer-reviewed journals. ChiCTR2600124496.

papers.title: Determination of central pain modulation biomarkers to characterise patients with cancer and refractory pain: protocol for a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Pain is one of the most prevalent and disabling oncological symptoms, but its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Most research has focused on peripheral mechanisms, while central pain modulation has been poorly explored. Quantitative sensory testing (QST) and electroencephalography (EEG) provide non-invasive approaches to assess central pain processing but the evidence using those approaches in patients with cancer is limited. This study protocol aims to identify and validate central biomarkers of pain perception and modulation (QST and EEG) and the role of moderator variables to better characterise patients with cancer pain. This study protocol describes a multicentre, cross-sectional, case-control study that will include a minimum of 470 ambulatory patients with cancer, including 313 with oncological pain and 157 without pain. Participants will be recruited taking into account age, sex and cancer type (lung, breast, pancreas, prostate and colon). All participants will perform a single face-to-face assessment that will include sociodemographic and clinical data, QST (pain modulation and inhibitory pain mechanisms, temporal summation and pain thresholds) and EEG (at rest and in response to thermal nociceptive stimuli) assessment and administration of questionnaires (pain, quality of life, fatigue, sleep, mood, etc). Statistical modelling and machine learning approaches will be used to investigate pain modulation biomarkers, their association with age and sex and to characterise patients with cancer pain. This study has received approval from all local ethics committees of the participating clinical sites. Results will be disseminated through high-impact peer-reviewed journals, international conferences and open data repositories, in compliance with General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles, and following the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) statement for observational case-control studies. ISRCTN35887998.

papers.title: Comparable memory retention following brief periods of wakeful rest and napping: A pilot study.
papers.abstract: Wakeful rest and sleep are both known to support memory retention. However, it remains unclear whether the benefits of wakeful rest are comparable to those of an equivalent period of sleep. To address this question, this study examined whether wakeful rest and sleep produce comparable behavioral effects and electrophysiological activity patterns. Ninety participants completed an incidental picture-encoding task and were then assigned to one of three 20-min delay conditions: wakeful rest, gameplay, or napping. After the delay, all participants completed an old/new recognition test that included lure pictures resembling previously encoded items. EEG was recorded during recognition. Behavioral results showed better general item memory after wakeful rest and napping than after gameplay, with no significant difference between the wakeful rest group (RG) and the nap group (NG). Bayesian equivalence testing provided moderate evidence in favor of comparable memory performance between the RG and NG. ERP analyses revealed similar FN400 and LPC patterns in both groups. Moreover, multivariate pattern analysis indicated broadly comparable old versus new decoding performance between the RG and NG, and cross-state decoding suggested that classification-relevant neural activity patterns were partially generalizable across the two groups. Overall, over a short post-encoding interval, general recognition memory retention following wakeful rest was comparable to that observed following a light nap.

papers.title: Anterior cingulate cortex glutamatergic projection neurons modulate motion sickness susceptibility via a cortico-vestibular circuit.
papers.abstract: Motion sickness (MS) is a prevalent and debilitating vestibular disorder with limited therapeutic options, yet the cortical mechanisms governing individual susceptibility remain elusive. Using a biaxial rotation mouse model, we investigated the role of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) in MS by integrating morphology, calcium imaging, electrophysiology, cell ablation, chemogenetics, and optogenetics. Biaxial rotation induced hypothermia, anorexia, taste avoidance, locomotor hypoactivity, and gait incoordination. ACC pyramidal neurons exhibited enhanced activation and increased intrinsic excitability following vestibular stimulation. Ablation of ACC CaMKII+ neurons alleviated MS symptoms, and bidirectional chemogenetic manipulation demonstrated that ACC glutamatergic projection neurons are both necessary and sufficient for MS behaviors. Furthermore, the ACC to medial vestibular nuclei parvicellular part (MVePC) projection was identified as a previously uncharacterized cortico-vestibular circuit that bidirectionally mediates MS susceptibility. Whole-brain projectome analysis further revealed anatomically heterogeneous projection subtypes of ACC-medial vestibular neurons. These findings advance our understanding of the cortical mechanisms underlying MS and establish the ACC-MVePC pathway as a mechanistic entry point for future neuromodulatory strategies.

papers.title: Characteristics of skeletal Class III subjects with and without obstructive sleep apnea.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the clinical, skeletal, pharyngeal airway, and sleep characteristics of skeletal Class III subjects with and without obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). A retrospective case-control study was conducted in 46 subjects (18 with OSA and 28 without OSA). Medical records, cephalometric analyses, cone-beam computed tomography, Thai versions of the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, modified STOP-Bang Questionnaire (SBQ), and sleep study results were evaluated. The OSA group predominantly comprised males and exhibited higher body mass index (BMI) and larger neck circumference. Sleep analysis showed that subjects with OSA had higher modified SBQ scores, higher snoring level, increased light sleep, and reduced REM sleep stages compared with non-OSA subjects. Among skeletal variables, only mandibular length (Go-Gn) was significantly shorter in the OSA group. Pharyngeal airway revealed a longer uvula, increased airway length, and narrower lateral dimensions of the upper segment of pharyngeal airway. Univariable analysis identified male sex, BMI >25 kg/m², neck circumference >40 cm, modified SBQ score ≥3, snoring, and mandibular length <80 mm as factors associated with OSA. In multivariable logistic regression analysis, male sex (adjusted OR = 8.11, 95%CI: 1.10-59.51, p = 0.040) and mandibular length <80 mm (adjusted OR = 8.40, 95%CI: 1.05-67.17, p = 0.045) remained significantly associated with OSA. Within skeletal Class III subjects, OSA was associated with male sex and shorter mandibular length, while differences in regional airway morphology were observed in the unadjusted analyses. Integrating clinical and imaging parameters may provide complementary information for identifying skeletal Class III patients at increased risk of OSA.
papers.journal: Journal of stomatology, oral and maxillofacial surgery

papers.title: Multi-Level Toxicity of 6PPD-Q and TiO2 Nanoparticles in Mytilus coruscus: Links among Neurochemical, Circadian and Metabolic Responses.
papers.abstract: Tire-derived 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q) and titanium dioxide nanoparticles (TiO2 NPs) are increasingly detected in aquatic environments, yet their combined effects on marine bivalves remain poorly understood. In this study, the thick-shell mussel Mytilus coruscus was exposed to 6PPD-Q, TiO2 NPs, and their mixtures to evaluate multi-level physiological, biochemical, histological, and molecular responses. The results demonstrated that 6PPD-Q and TiO2 NPs, particularly under high-concentration co-exposure, significantly impaired mussel physiological performance, as indicated by reduced clearance rate and O:N ratio, increased oxygen consumption and excretion rate, and pronounced gill histopathological injury. Co-exposure also caused clear energy metabolic disruption, including decreased ATP content and inhibited CS, LDH, and PK activities, together with suppressed neurotransmitter levels of DA, ACh, and GABA. In addition, the expression patterns of circadian rhythm- and metabolism-related genes, including CRY, Per2, PPARγ, ACO, and PEPCK, were markedly altered, suggesting disruption of neuro-circadian-metabolic regulation. Oxidative stress was evident in both gills and digestive gland, as reflected by altered CAT and SOD activities and elevated MDA levels. These responses were accompanied by significant modulation of inflammatory and apoptotic genes, including TNF-α, IL-17, TGF-β, Caspase-3, Caspase-8, and Bcl-2. These findings suggest that 6PPD-Q and TiO2 NPs may jointly impair mussel health by linking gill first-contact injury with metabolic dysregulation, oxidative stress, and immune-apoptotic damage.

papers.title: Vitamin B6 augments antidepressant activity of venlafaxine by restoring cortical EEG oscillations, behavior and oxidative biomarkers in chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-induced model of depression-like behavior.
papers.abstract: Depression is a multifactorial neuropsychiatric disorder associated with chronic stress, disrupted neural oscillations and oxidative stress. The present study investigated whether vitamin B6 (Vit B6) enhances the antidepressant efficacy of venlafaxine (VEN) in a chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-induced model of depression-like behavior in C57BL/6 mice. A total of 72 mice, divided into two subsets, i.e., with and without EEG electrodes, were treated with VEN and Vit B6 alone and in combination for 28 days. The EEG electrode-bearing mice were tested for electrophysiological changes on day 29. Mice without EEG electrodes were tested for behavioral changes during days 29-32, followed by brain isolation on day 33 for biochemical analysis. The CUMS control demonstrated weight loss, anxiety-like activity in light/dark box, and depression-like behavior in sucrose splash, tail suspension and forced swim tests. Moreover, the EEG showed increased theta and reduced alpha and gamma activity. Further, CUMS resulted in marked elevation in brain oxidative stress in terms of elevated malondialdehyde (MDA) and reduced catalase activity. Monotherapy with VEN and Vit B6 partially mitigated these alterations, but the combined treatment restored behavioral performance in light/dark test with increased grooming in the sucrose splash test, while reducing immobility in the tail suspension and forced swim tests. Biochemically, the combined therapy reduced oxidative stress in the brain by reducing MDA and increasing catalase activity. Additionally, the EEG evaluation revealed the restoration of cortical oscillations, attenuation of theta hyperactivity, and increased alpha and gamma band power, indicating improved neuronal synchronization. The study's outcomes suggest that combining vitamin B6 with venlafaxine enhances its antidepressant effects, possibly by modulating oxidative stress and neural circuitry. This combination strategy might be a promising approach to improve therapeutic outcomes in stress-associated depressive disorder.

papers.title: Lifestyle determinants of glycemic responses to snacking in free-living adults without diabetes: an intensive longitudinal observational study.
papers.abstract: Snacking is common and can contribute to blood glucose fluctuations. However, large studies investigating lifestyle determinants of glucose responses to snacking under real-world conditions are scarce. In this intensive longitudinal observational study, we analyzed data from 3,325 snacking episodes captured by ecological momentary assessment surveys (six daily), continuous glucose monitoring, and accelerometry over nine free-living days among 785 male and female adults aged 21-69 years without diabetes in Singapore. Postprandial glucose responses were assessed using 2-hour postprandial glucose incremental area under the curve (iAUC) following snacking episodes. Lifestyle exposures included consumption of snack foods and beverages, snack timing, postprandial physical activity, and daily physical activity and sleep prior to snacking episodes. Linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate within-person and between-person associations between these exposures and 2-hour postprandial glucose iAUC. The average 2-hour postprandial glucose iAUC was 63.8 (SD: 61.8) mmol/l*minute after snacking episodes. Consumption of bread or buns (within-person β: 30.7; 95% CI: 20.4, 41.1), deep-fried foods (β: 19.8; CI: 9.2, 30.4), sweets (β: 14.6; CI: 6.6, 22.6), and sugary beverages (β: 12.2; CI: 4.3, 20.0) was associated with higher glucose iAUC. In contrast, greater postprandial moderate-to-vigorous physical activity was associated with a lower glucose iAUC (β: -28.4 per hour; CI: -49.2, -7.5). In addition, glucose iAUC was higher following afternoon snacking (β: 9.3; CI: 2.0, 16.6) and early evening (β: 10.7; CI: 2.5, 18.9) than morning snacking. Snack composition, snack timing, and postprandial physical activity were associated with postprandial glucose responses to snacking in adults without diabetes. Recommendations on snacking-related lifestyle behaviors may improve glycemic control in daily life.
papers.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition

papers.title: Distinct behavioral and electrophysiological correlates of sleep disturbance during verbal and spatial working memory tasks.
papers.abstract: Associations between sleep disturbance and working memory (WM) vary across tasks and outcome measures. This study examined behavioral and electrophysiological correlates of subjective sleep disturbance during verbal working memory (VWM) and spatial working memory (SWM) in university students. Sixty-one participants were classified using Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores into a sleep disturbance group (n = 28) and a normal sleep group (n = 33) and completed separate verbal and spatial 2-back tasks with event-related potential (ERP) recording. After adjustment for depression, anxiety, and stress, the sleep disturbance group showed lower VWM accuracy (ACC) (mean difference = -3.89 percentage points, 95% CI [-6.83, -0.96]) and discrimination sensitivity (d'). VWM false alarm rates (FAR) were also higher, although the absolute difference was small. Higher PSQI scores were associated with lower VWM ACC and d' and higher FAR. The sleep disturbance group showed lower VWM P3 amplitude averaged across the analyzed electrode sites and longer P3 peak latency at Oz. No significant group-related effects were detected for VWM median reaction time or N2 measures, or for SWM behavioral and ERP measures. These findings link subjective sleep disturbance to lower ACC and discrimination during verbal updating, accompanied by differences in later task-related electrophysiological processing. Future longitudinal and intervention studies with matched tasks and objective sleep measures could clarify the temporal and causal relationships underlying these associations.

papers.title: Exploring the Reconfiguration Effects of Physical Fatigue on the Gradient Space of Brain Function Based on EEG.
papers.abstract: This study examined how physical fatigue reorganizes the low-dimensional structure of EEG functional connectivity using three embedding approaches. Thirty male participants completed a Bruce treadmill test to exhaustion, with resting-state EEG recorded before and after exercise. Frequency-specific wPLI connectivity matrices were analyzed using PCA, Laplacian eigenmaps, and diffusion maps with common-reference alignment. Regional G1-G3 scores, G1-G2 displacement, λ1-λ3 eigenvalues, and their associations with exercise duration were assessed. PCA showed increased beta-band G1 scores over the central scalp region and decreased scores over the occipital region, together with reduced alpha-band G3 over the central region. LE showed increased theta-band G3 over the central region. PCA displacement exhibited a significant frequency band × scalp region interaction, driven by greater alpha-band occipital displacement. Theta-band λ1-λ3 increased with PCA but decreased with DM, whereas LE showed no significant eigenvalue changes. The PCA-derived beta-band central ΔG1 was positively correlated with exhaustive exercise duration (r = 0.50, p = 0.004). Physical fatigue induces frequency-, region-, component-, and method-specific reorganization of the low-dimensional structure of scalp-level EEG functional connectivity. PCA was particularly sensitive to spatially differentiated gradient changes, while LE and DM captured complementary aspects of fatigue-related reorganization. The association between central beta-band ΔG1 and exercise duration further suggests potential behavioral relevance of gradient.

papers.title: From emotional inhibition to memory suppression: Acute exercise modulates electrophysiological dynamics associated with inhibitory control during suppression of negative memories.
papers.abstract: Failures in inhibitory control over negative emotional memories can lead to intrusive recollections that interfere with cognitive functioning and well-being. The present study examined whether acute exercise modulates the electrophysiological dynamics underlying inhibitory control during the suppression of negative emotional memories. Seventy healthy participants were randomly assigned to an acute exercise group or a seated-rest control group. The exercise group completed 30 min of moderate-intensity exercise, whereas the control group remained seated at rest. Participants completed the emotional Think/No-Think paradigm both before and after the intervention, while electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded. Event-related potentials (ERPs), time-frequency analyses, and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) were used to characterize neural processes associated with inhibitory control. Results showed that acute exercise selectively modulated late-stage neural activity during negative memory suppression, particularly within the 2400-3000 ms time window. This modulation was most evident over central site and left parietal site, and was accompanied by changes in alpha- and beta-band power at the left parieto-occipital junction. Overall, these findings suggest that acute exercise modulates late-stage neural dynamics during the suppression of negative memories. The observed neural changes were accompanied by a reduction in intrusion frequency during suppression attempts, consistent with the possibility that acute exercise facilitates late-stage sustained inhibition.
papers.journal: International journal of psychophysiology : official journal of the International Organization of Psychophysiology

papers.title: Bioimpedance-Derived Hydration and Body Composition Shifts Across Ramadan in Competitive Swimmers Aged 6-20 Years: A Prospective Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Ramadan fasting can alter hydration, sleep, and training schedules in competitive swimmers aged 6-20 years, but evidence in swimmers is limited. This prospective cohort study investigated within-participant changes in bioelectrical impedance analysis and body composition across Ramadan in swimmers. Swimmers were assessed at 3 time points: approximately 7 days before the first day of Ramadan, during the third week of Ramadan, and approximately 14 days after Ramadan ended. Participants were 52 competitive swimmers aged 6-20 years (39 males). Phase-sensitive single-frequency bioelectrical impedance analysis (50 kHz) measured phase angle (A50) and resistance (R50); derived outcomes included fat-free mass, fat mass, and body mass index. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age and sex estimated changes versus baseline with false discovery rate control. R50 increased during (+50 Ω) and after Ramadan (+42 Ω), fat-free mass decreased (-1.86 kg and -1.41 kg), fat mass increased (+1.29 kg and +1.68 kg), A50 declined modestly after Ramadan (-0.38°), and body mass index showed no clear change. Effects were directionally consistent across sex and fasting-type subgroups. Across Ramadan, swimmers aged 6-20 years exhibited higher electrical resistance and unfavorable shifts in body composition despite stable body mass index, consistent with transient hydration/cellular stress and possible tissue-related changes that cannot be confirmed without functional or regional measures. Routine bioelectrical impedance analysis-based monitoring and targeted evening hydration, protein distribution, and light resistance training may help preserve fat-free mass during Ramadan.

papers.title: 4-methyl-3-aminopyridine: A novel active blocker of voltage-gated potassium ion channels in the central nervous system.
papers.abstract: Aminopyridines, including 4-aminopyridine (4AP), 3,4-diaminopyridine, and [18F]3-fluoro-4-aminopyridine, are voltage-gated potassium (KV) channel blockers used clinically to enhance conduction in neurological disorders and to image demyelination by positron emission tomography (PET). Developing new aminopyridines may yield improved therapeutics or imaging agents. Here, we characterized the physicochemical properties (, ), KV channel-blocking activity, toxicity (), and pharmacokinetics of a novel compound, 4-methyl-3-aminopyridine (4Me3AP). 4Me3AP was less basic and more lipophilic than 4AP and showed greater blocking potency across multiple KV channels expressed in Xenopus oocytes. In mice, 4Me3AP exhibited lower acute toxicity ( = 29.3 mg/kg) than 4AP ( = 12.7 mg/kg) and a longer plasma half-life. These findings indicate that 4Me3AP is a potent KV channel blocker with favorable pharmacological properties, supporting its potential for symptomatic treatment of demyelinating diseases.

papers.title: Ordered onset of regional desynchronization and a transition in movement-class discriminability during cue-paced motor imagery.
papers.abstract: Motor imagery recruits a distributed sensorimotor network, yet the order in which its regions are engaged has not been tested statistically within the healthy brain, and the interval in which information about the imagined movement appears remains unidentified. Early post-cue classification peaks have been attributed to visually induced orienting rather than to imagery, an inference drawn from a condition contrast rather than direct measurement.Two independent public datasets were analysed under a matched pipeline of causal filtering, ocular regression and current source density: Weibo2014 as the primary dataset and BCI Competition IV dataset 2a for validation. Mu and beta desynchronization onset was ordered across cortex, from occipital through sensorimotor and midline pre-supplementary motor area to lateral prefrontal. The ordering held under all nine onset criteria examined, under channel-count matching and within-trial pairing, and after removal of the sensorimotor component. Class-discriminative information rose most steeply between 0.60 and 0.75 s and saturated within a further 0.3 s. This transition lay closer to sensorimotor onset than to cue presentation in every participant and fell at or after that onset in nearly all of them, although the two were not shown equivalent at the resolution of the decoding grid. Windows centred on each region's own onset classified equivalently to reassigned windows, so the ordering serves as a temporal landmark rather than a decodable feature, locating the interval in which information about the imagined movement becomes available.

papers.title: Sleep Problems and Mental Health in Middle-Aged and Older Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults.
papers.abstract: Sleep is a vital biological function, and impaired sleep can lead to a range of problems, including poor health and wellbeing. Poor sleep and higher rates of sleep-related problems and difficulties are often reported by autistic people of all ages, however, these experiences and problems have seldom been studied in diagnosed autistic populations in midlife and old age. This study used data from the first wave of the AgeWellAutism cohort, from a sample of 265 autistic and 167 age- and gender-matched non-autistic adults aged 40-93 years (mean = ∼60 years; ∼50% female). Participants completed widely used and standardised measures of sleep quality and mental health symptoms. The autistic group reported significantly greater sleep problems than the non-autistic group, with poorer overall sleep across all domains (all p < 0.001), with autistic women reporting greatest difficulties. The largest differences between groups were observed in sleep disturbances and daytime dysfunction (χ2 = 101.8 and 95.1, respectively, both p < 0.001). These differences remained significant after controlling for age and symptoms of anxiety, depression and PTSD. Across both groups, poorer sleep was associated with older age and higher levels of anxiety, depression and PTSD symptoms, with a stronger association between sleep problems and anxiety symptoms in the autistic group. Consistent with prior autism trait-based research in the general population, middle-aged and older autistic adults report more extensive sleep problems and worse sleep quality than non-autistic adults. Sleep problems were associated with older age and poorer mental health. Though the study is cross-sectional, the findings highlight the need to explore causal links through intervention. Addressing anxiety, and mental health problems more broadly, may improve sleep quality in ageing autistic populations.

papers.title: Postoperative symptom burden and factors associated with health-related quality of life within six months after pancreatic cancer surgery in middle-aged and older adults.
papers.abstract: To examine the simultaneous associations of postoperative pain, anxiety, and sleep quality with functional health-related quality of life (HRQOL), symptom burden, and global health status among middle-aged and older adults within six months after pancreatic cancer surgery. This cross-sectional study included 151 patients aged ≥45 years who had undergone pancreatic cancer surgery within the preceding six months. Pain, anxiety, sleep quality, and HRQOL were assessed using the Numeric Rating Scale, the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-Anxiety subscale, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, and the EORTC QLQ-C30, respectively. Pearson correlations and hierarchical multiple regression analyses were conducted. Mean pain, anxiety, and sleep-quality scores were 5.04 ± .58, 8.41 ± 3.33, and 9.81 ± 3.97, respectively. Anxiety was correlated with poorer functional HRQOL (r = -.43), greater symptom burden (r = .38), and poorer global health status (r = -.32; all P < .001). Poorer sleep quality was also associated with all three domains (r = -.39 to .47; all P < .001). Pain was correlated only with symptom burden (r = .19, P < .05). In fully adjusted models, anxiety remained associated with functional HRQOL (β = -.323, P < .001), symptom burden (β = .208, P = .005), and global health status (β = -.194, P = .019); sleep quality showed corresponding associations (β = -.241, P = .003; β = .326, P < .001; β = -.290, P = .001). Pain remained associated only with symptom burden (β = .184, P = .008). Anxiety and poor sleep quality were consistently associated with poorer HRQOL outcomes after pancreatic cancer surgery. Routine assessment of these symptoms may help identify patients requiring additional supportive care.
papers.journal: European journal of oncology nursing : the official journal of European Oncology Nursing Society

papers.title: Indoor environmental conditions and interictal epileptiform discharge frequency during pediatric video-EEG monitoring.
papers.abstract: To characterize the effects of short-term fluctuations in indoor temperature/humidity during inpatient monitoring of children with epilepsy. We evaluated 50 paediatric patients (mean age 10.3 years; 56% focal epilepsy, 30% generalized, 14% combined) with continuous, minute-level serial data to assess the relationships between environmental parameters (temperature, relative humidity, dew point) and epileptiform discharge frequency. Both contemporary and lagged (1-hour, 6-hour) individual-level correlation analyses and Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMM) were performed to examine environmental responsiveness alongside clinical variables. At evaluation, 68% of patients had ongoing seizures, and 90% received antiseizure therapy. Individual-level analyses revealed widespread heterogeneity in environmental responsiveness. Following FDR correction, statistically significant correlations with temperature and relative humidity were observed in 37/50 patients each, with correlation coefficients spanning bidirectional ranges from strongly negative to strongly positive. Lagged temperature, lagged humidity, and dew point yielded similarly heterogeneous, significant individual associations. Conversely, GLMM group-level analysis demonstrated a significant circadian effect on interictal discharge rates, while linear/quadratic environmental terms and clinical characteristics (epilepsy duration, seizure status, therapy, and epilepsy type) showed no statistically significant group-level effects or moderation. Pediatric epilepsy patients exhibit marked, highly individualized bidirectional sensitivities to ambient temperature and humidity despite a uniform group-level circadian rhythm in cortical excitability. These findings underscore the importance of personalized environmental monitoring in epilepsy management.

papers.title: Human in silico modeling guided by transcriptomics predicts drug-induced proarrhythmicity as a function of age.
papers.abstract: Unexpected cardiotoxicity is a major cause of drug failure during development and can also contribute to market withdrawal. Traditional preclinical models and clinical trials do not fully capture age-related cardiac functional decline, which is associated with increased arrhythmic risk. We aimed to develop human-based in silico electrophysiology models incorporating age-related remodeling to improve the assessment of age-dependent drug-induced cardiotoxicity during drug development. Biological and chronological transcriptomic age-related human ventricular ionic remodeling was integrated into the O'Hara-Virag-Varro-Rudy model of ventricular electrophysiology at both cellular and tissue levels. Cardiac biological age was represented using two independent gene expression-based indices: SenesAge, based on one gene related to cell senescence, and AppAge, based on nearly 2,000 age-related genes. A panel of 12 reference drugs was used to evaluate age-related drug-induced cardiotoxicity. In silico aging based on SenesAge and AppAge reproduced age-related electrophysiological phenotypes at the cellular, tissue, and ECG levels more closely than chronological age-based remodeling. Biological age-related remodeling also increased the susceptibility to arrhythmogenic events following drug exposure by more than fivefold with respect to the adult population across the majority of tested conditions, although the effects varied according to the drug and its concentration. This study provides a novel perspective for incorporating biological age-related remodeling into an established human-based in silico framework for preclinical cardiotoxicity evaluation at the population level. Our findings support biological age-based modeling as a complement to chronological age-based approaches for improving age-specific drug-induced cardiac risk assessment.
papers.journal: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine

papers.title: Rethinking the lexicon of REM sleep behavior disorder: a two-axis proposal.
papers.abstract: REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia occurring during REM sleep, with different etiologies. The current international lexicon identifies a clinically oriented definition, which is 'clinically isolated RBD', when a clear causative disorder is not identified, and a pathophysiology-based definition, termed 'secondary RBD', when a known cause of RBD is evident. However, these two terms reflect different aspects of the disease and may be misleading and confusing, especially when defining disorders biologically, e.g., with biomarkers. This viewpoint proposes a new RBD lexicon based on evidence from the literature. The proposal envisions a two-axis framework integrating a pathophysiological and a clinical axis to classify polysomnography-confirmed RBD more coherently than the current, possibly misleading terminology. We suggest that this framework may improve patient description in both clinical and research settings, thereby enhancing patient characterization and clinical transparency.

papers.title: Neural correlates of phi and reverse-phi motion aftereffects: Temporal dynamics of ON-OFF pathway interactions.
papers.abstract: Sensory processing is dynamically shaped by neural adaptation, allowing the brain to adjust to recent sensory input. Phi and reverse-phi motion provide a framework for probing adaptive processes and ON-OFF pathway interactions in visual motion processing. We recorded 64-channel EEG while 30 participants completed a rapid motion-adaptation paradigm. Participants adapted to contrast-preserving phi motion or contrast-reversing reverse-phi motion for a short (188 msec) or long (752 msec) duration and then judged the direction of an ambiguous counterphase-flickering test grating. Behaviourally, adaptation duration primarily determined perceptual bias: short adaptation produced a modest same-direction, priming-like bias, whereas long adaptation produced an opposite-direction motion aftereffect. Test-locked event-related potentials (ERPs) revealed a robust Duration × Adaptation Type interaction over early posterior scalp regions (128-160 msec), primarily expressed in the N1 range. This interaction reflected greater differentiation between phi and reverse-phi adaptation after long than short adaptation. Exploratory whole-scalp topographic analyses indicated that the interaction involved changes in scalp-response configuration rather than uniform amplitude modulation. Adapter-locked analyses further showed that phi and reverse-phi motion elicited distinguishable ERP responses during the initial adaptation period and separable multivariate EEG patterns from approximately 50 msec after adapter onset, indicating early neural divergence between the two motion types. Together, these findings provide electrophysiological evidence that rapid adaptation to phi and reverse-phi motion leaves distinct neural traces that differentially influence subsequent processing of an ambiguous motion stimulus, advancing our understanding of rapid sensory adaptation and ON-OFF pathway interactions in human motion perception.
papers.journal: Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior

papers.title: Developmental variation in resting-state EEG spectral correlates of response inhibition in children and adolescents.
papers.abstract: Identifying electrophysiological markers of response inhibition in children and adolescents is of substantial importance. Although previous studies have examined associations between resting-state electroencephalography (rs-EEG) power and response inhibition, findings across frequency bands have been inconsistent, and evidence regarding band-ratio indices remains limited. To address these issues, the present study examined the associations between rs-EEG spectral indices and response inhibition in a large sample of 1654 children and adolescents aged 6-18 years, and further tested whether these associations varied as a function of age. Based on eyes-open rs-EEG recordings, relative power was extracted for the delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands, and three band-ratio indices were calculated: the theta/beta ratio (TBR), alpha/theta ratio (ATR), and beta/theta ratio (BTR). Response inhibition was assessed using the stop-signal task. Correlation analyses showed that higher delta power, theta power, and TBR were associated with poorer response inhibition, whereas higher alpha power, beta power, ATR, and BTR were associated with better response inhibition. Moderation analyses further indicated that age significantly moderated the associations of delta power, beta power, ATR, and BTR with response inhibition, whereas no significant age-moderating effects were observed for theta power, alpha power or TBR. Taken together, these findings suggest that the electrophysiological correlates of response inhibition are developmentally dynamic across childhood and adolescence. The present study provides a psychophysiological account of developmental variation in response inhibition and underscores the importance of age when interpreting resting-state EEG-behavior associations.

papers.title: A systematic review of digital and wearable sensor data in the ABCD study: Insights, methods, and emerging opportunities.
papers.abstract: Research into key adolescent health domains, like problematic screen-based media use, sleep health, and physical activity, are frequently limited by error-prone self-report-based measures. To improve the measurement of such behaviors, the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study (ABCD), a diverse longitudinal cohort study of nearly 12,000 U.S. youth (ages 9-10 at Baseline), includes remote sensing protocols during data collection. Consenting participants provided up to three weeks of Fitbit actigraphy data, beginning at the year-two follow up, and smartphone usage data, beginning at the year-four follow up, collected via the Effortless Assessment of Research Systems (EARS) smartphone application. This systematic review aimed to identify and synthesize all published empirical studies which have utilized the ABCD Study's passive sensor data, identifying 45 articles investigating measurement validity, and associations with adolescent health, development, and neurocognitive functioning. Fitbit devices broadly reproduced estimates of sleep and physical activity obtained from research-grade sensors. Smartphone sensor data were internally consistent, reproduced expected daily usage patterns, and were moderately correlated with self-report. Most substantive studies utilized Fitbit data and reported cross-sectional associations between sensor-derived single-item summary statistics and survey-based measures of mental and behavioral health, neurocognitive functioning, or environmental risk factors. A smaller number of studies utilized longitudinal designs, within-person analyses, machine learning approaches, and/or genetic or neuroimaging methods to reduce confounding and enhance biological and etiological insight into these observed relationships. While published findings were largely incremental in nature, ABCD's passive sensing resources nonetheless represent a powerful, widely available resource for incorporating sensor-based measures into adolescent health research.

papers.title: Visual classification of nocturnal transcutaneous CO2 and oximetry patterns in slowly progressive neuromuscular diseases: a derivation and feasibility study.
papers.abstract: Sleep-disordered breathing is highly prevalent in subjects with neuromuscular diseases (NMD). We hypothesized that visual analysis of nocturnal transcutaneous CO2 (TcCO2) monitoring could help physicians identify distinct respiratory phenotypes. This study aimed to derive a visual classification of nocturnal transcutaneous CO2 and oximetry patterns in patients with slowly progressive neuromuscular diseases and to assess its feasibility and inter-rater agreement. Retrospective study of 149 NMD subjects, naive to noninvasive ventilation, who underwent full-night TcCO2 monitoring. Three investigators independently reviewed each TcCO2 tracing and assigned a profile: absence of nocturnal hypercapnia (NH-), clusters of hypercapnic peaks only (cluNH), constant nocturnal hypercapnia without clusters (ConNH), and constant nocturnal hypercapnia associated with clusters (ConNH with cluNH). Profiles were also derived from the SpO2 tracing: absence or presence of an oxygen drop with a sawtooth profile (OD- or OD+). Overlap was defined as any form of nocturnal hypercapnia associated with OD+. Final classification was based on majority agreement, with consensus adjudication when no majority existed. Inter-rater agreement was assessed. Each profile was compared in terms of demographic data and parameters from arterial blood gases, pulmonary function testing, and respiratory polygraphy. Overall agreement was kappa = 0.68 (95% CI, 0.61-0.75) for TcCO2 classification and kappa = 0.55 (95% CI, 0.44-0.65) for OD-/OD+, with complete agreement in 71.1% and 72.5% of recordings, respectively. Agreement was moderate for hypercapnic clusters and the sawtooth pattern. After correction, hypercapnic profiles remained associated with lower vital and supine vital capacities and higher daytime PaCO2 and bicarbonate than NH-, OD + remained associated with a higher apnea-hypopnea index. Visual classification of overnight TcCO2 and SpO2 recordings was feasible and showed moderate inter-rater agreement for hypercapnic clusters and the sawtooth oximetry pattern. The visual profiles were associated with selected physiological characteristics, but these associations primarily support face validity. Prospective external validation is required to determine whether this classification provides information beyond conventional quantitative indices or improves clinical decision-making.

papers.title: High arousal threshold is associated with impaired sustained attention in patients with obstructive sleep apnea.
papers.abstract: Impaired sustained attention is common in patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but the influencing factors are unclear. OSA patients with high Arousal threshold (ArTH) often experience severer hypoxia, possibly worsening sustained attention. To determine the association between ArTH and sustained attention in OSA. OSA was defined as apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) ≥5 events/hour in polysomnography. ArTH was scored using three criteria (1 point each): 1) AHI<30 events/hour, 2) minimum peripheral oxygen saturation >82.5%, and 3) hypopnea proportion >58.3%. High and low ArTH was defined as 0-1 and ≥2 points respectively. Sustained attention was evaluated by Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT). Impaired sustained attention manifested as higher lapse probability, slower mean 1/reaction time (RT), slower slowest 10% 1/RT, and slower fastest 10% 1/RT. We included 97 OSA patients, with 59 high and 38 low ArTH patients. High ArTH group exhibited higher lapse probability (15.08±3.12 vs. 4.72±1.61%, p=0.004), lower slowest 10% 1/RT (1.76±0.09 vs. 2.06±0.07 s-1, p=0.009), mean 1/RT (2.77±0.09 vs. 3.05±0.05 s-1, p=0.008), fastest 10% 1/RT (3.64±0.10 vs. 3.86±0.06 s-1, p=0.068) with adjustment of age, gender, and overweight. These results remained similar after additionally adjusting education levels and percentages of non-rapid eye movement sleep stage 3. Linear trends were observed between lower ArTH scores and higher lapse probability (p-for-trend=0.015), lower slowest 10% 1/RT (p-for-trend=0.009), mean 1/RT (p-for-trend=0.010) and fastest 10% 1/RT (p-for-trend=0.092). High ArTH may be associated with impaired sustained attention in OSA patients. Assessing ArTH may help identify OSA patients at high risk for attention impairment.
papers.journal: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care

papers.title: Impact of obstructive sleep apnea on outcomes of acute respiratory distress syndrome: propensity matched analysis of a national cohort.
papers.abstract: The effects of co-existing OSA on the outcomes of ARDS are unclear. This retrospective study aimed to compare the outcomes and resource utilization rates of OSA patients who develop ARDS with a matched control group. Adult patients hospitalized between 2016 and 2019 with a diagnostic code for ARDS were identified within the Nationwide Inpatient Sample. Patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema were excluded. By utilizing propensity score calculations, patients with OSA were individually matched with and compared to patients without OSA. Primary outcomes were mortality, length of stay and total hospitalization charges. 9405 OSA patients were matched with 9206 controls. OSA was independently associated with 34% lower odds of in-hospital mortality (21.1%vs 24.9%; aOR 0.66, 95% CI 0.61-0.72; p < 0.001), shorter length of stay (B - 2.0 days; p < 0.001), and lower total hospitalization charges (B -$74,601; P < 0.001). OSA patients had lower rates of invasive mechanical ventilation (aOR 0.79; p < 0.001) and tracheostomy (aOR 0.66; p < 0.001) but higher noninvasive ventilation use (aOR 1.40; p < 0.001). In a subgroup analysis of OSA patients, NIV was associated with fewer tracheostomies (aOR 0.61; p < 0.001) and lower charges (B -$26,625; p < 0.001) but was not associated with mortality or length of stay. In this nationally representative cohort, preexisting OSA was paradoxically associated with lower mortality, shorter hospitalization, and reduced resource utilization in ARDS. These findings suggest possible protective mechanisms warranting further prospective investigation.
papers.journal: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care

papers.title: From pathogenesis to non-medical therapy: A review of exploring sensory and multi-sensory stimulation as a non-invasive treatment approach for Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, marked by the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, tau pathology, and synaptic dysfunction, ultimately leading to memory loss, cognitive decline, neuropsychiatric symptoms and neuronal degeneration that impairs daily functioning. Despite the availability of pharmacological treatments developed to slow down symptom progression, their clinical efficacy remains uncertain, and they are frequently associated with adverse side effects, underscoring the urgent demand for safer and more effective therapeutic alternatives. Non-pharmacological approaches, therefore, have been investigated and are considered promising alternative therapeutic strategies for AD. This paper outlines the pathological features and neural network changes that occur across the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD), reviews the effects of different sensory stimulation approaches on reducing these AD-associated changes, and discusses the potential mechanisms underlying various sensory and multisensory stimulation interventions in mitigating AD-related symptoms. These sensory stimulation interventions, including 40 Hz Gamma Entrainment Using Sensory Stimulation [GENUS], Photobiomodulation, Bright Light Therapy, Music Therapy, Aromatherapy, Tactile Stimulation, and Multisensory Stimulation, are found to slow down the progression of AD by ameliorating multiple AD pathologies, enhancing cognitive function, promoting neuroplasticity, regulating sleep patterns, and reducing behavioural or neuropsychiatric symptoms. Crucially, this present work integrates both human and animal studies, aligning clinical outcomes with mechanistic insights derived from animal studies, thereby bridging preclinical and clinical research to promote the translation of sensory interventions into effective treatments for patients with AD.

papers.title: EEG predictors of transition from clinical high risk to psychotic disorders: A systematic review with implications for data harmonisation.
papers.abstract: Prognostic markers of transition from a clinical high-risk (CHR) state to psychosis are important for intervention. Although electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) abnormalities are associated with psychotic disorders, their prognostic utility in CHR populations remains unclear. This systematic review examined EEG and MEG differences between CHR individuals who transitioned to psychosis (CHR-T) and those who did not (CHR-NT). Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, APA PsycINFO, APA PsycArticles, CINAHL Ultimate, Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection were searched for studies published from January 1990 to July 2026. Backward citation searches of included publications and reviews supplemented database searches. Eligible studies compared baseline EEG or MEG measures between CHR-T and CHR-NT groups. Findings were narratively synthesised because of heterogeneity, study quality was assessed using Quality in Prognosis Studies (QUIPS), and event-related potential (ERP) data were meta-analysed where comparable. Out of 613 records screened, 52 publications met inclusion criteria. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted by ERP subtype. The clearest pooled differences were observed for duration MMN (k = 9, Hedges' g = 0.49, 95% CI [0.14, 0.83]) and P3b (k = 5, g = -0.61, 95% CI [-0.97, -0.25]), both reduced in CHR-T compared to CHR-NT. Other subtype analyses included few studies and produced mixed findings. Achieving reliable predictive sensitivity from EEG biomarkers is difficult during the clinically and diagnostically heterogeneous CHR period. Inconsistency across EEG methodologies and outcome definitions likely contributes to variability in reported prognostic effects. Recommendations are provided to improve methodological consistency and support future biomarker research.

papers.title: Melatonin protects keratinocytes from diesel-derived PM2.5-induced damage by suppressing JNK/p38 MAPK signaling and caspase activation.
papers.abstract: Melatonin is a naturally produced hormone in the human body that primarily regulates the sleep-wake cycle. This study examined the role of melatonin in protecting human keratinocytes from diesel-derived particulate matter 2.5 (DPM2.5)-induced oxidative injury. HaCaT keratinocytes and male HR-1 hairless mice were exposed to DPM2.5 to induce oxidative injury and treated with various concentrations of melatonin, followed by various analyses, including reactive oxygen species (ROS) detection, mitochondrial membrane potential analysis, western blotting, and cell cycle analysis. Melatonin exhibited potent radical-scavenging activity. Consistently, melatonin attenuated DPM2.5-induced intracellular ROS, mitigated oxidative damage to cellular macromolecules, and restored cell viability. Furthermore, melatonin reduced DPM2.5-induced apoptotic cell death by alleviating mitochondrial dysfunction, including mitochondrial membrane potential disruption. It also partially restored the decreased Bcl-2 expression and increased Bax and Bim expression in DPM2.5-treated cells, suppressing DPM2.5-induced activation of caspase-9 and caspase-3. Given that ROS overproduction is a key activator of c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK)/p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling, we determined whether melatonin-mediated antioxidant effects are linked to suppression of these pathways. Melatonin reduced DPM2.5-mediated JNK and p38 MAPK phosphorylation, and protective effects were observed in DPM2.5-exposed mouse skin tissue. Particularly, co-treatment of melatonin with pan-caspase, JNK, or p38 MAPK inhibitors did not significantly alter the anti-apoptotic effect of melatonin in DPM2.5-treated cells. In conclusion, melatonin protects human keratinocytes from DPM2.5-induced oxidative stress damage by scavenging ROS, thereby mitigating damage to cellular components. It also reduces damage to skin keratinocytes from DPM2.5-induced apoptosis by inhibiting caspase- and/or MAPK-dependent signaling pathways. Thus, melatonin has potential as an active ingredient for developing skin-care products to prevent the harmful effects of DPM2.5.

papers.title: A multidimensional, person-centered measure of menopausal symptom impact: Development and validation of the Menopause Impact Scale (MIS).
papers.abstract: To develop and validate the Menopause Impact Scale (MIS), a brief, person-centered measure of menopause-related symptom impact that is psychometrically robust across reproductive stages and suitable for digital implementation. Three sequential online studies with women aged 21-85 years in the United States (total N = 2915). Study 1 (n = 486) evaluated a 57-item pool using exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and reliability indices. Study 2 (n = 1429) used confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and item reduction to derive a brief scale. Study 3 (n = 1000) cross-validated the final structure and examined convergent and divergent validity, age sensitivity, and menopause etiology differences. MIS total and subscale scores; structural fit indices; internal consistency; convergent validity with the Greene Climacteric Scale; divergent validity with the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory; age group and menopause etiology differences in symptom burden. EFA supported a seven-factor solution (Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy [KMO] = 0.968; root-mean-square error of approximation [RMSEA] = 0.048; Cronbach's α = 0.974). A 22-item model showed excellent fit in Study 2 (comparative fit index [CFI] = 0.970; RMSEA = 0.047; α = 0.964) and was confirmed in Study 3 (CFI = 0.977; RMSEA = 0.041; α = 0.941), capturing cognitive, self-perception, sexual/vaginal, musculoskeletal, vasomotor, sleep, and urinary domains. Convergent validity with the Greene total score was strong (r = 0.76); divergent validity with burnout was moderate (r = 0.57). MIS scores peaked in midlife (45-55 years). After age adjustment, symptom burden was highest in primary ovarian insufficiency, with the largest differences in vasomotor and genitourinary domains. The MIS is a brief, multidimensional, impact-focused instrument with strong structural, convergent, and discriminant validity, supporting research, clinical, and digital applications.

papers.title: AI-Driven and Automated Systems for Continuous Oxygen Saturation Monitoring in Long-Term Oxygen Therapy: Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) improves outcomes in selected patients with severe chronic hypoxemia, but conventional LTOT uses fixed oxygen flow prescriptions that may not reflect changing needs during activity, sleep, or exacerbations. AI and automated oxygen systems may support continuous peripheral capillary oxygen saturation (SpO2) monitoring, signal-quality assessment, and adaptive oxygen titration. Evidence comparing AI-driven and non-AI automated approaches across performance, clinical readiness, LTOT applicability, and equity remains limited. This systematic review synthesized peer-reviewed evidence on AI-driven and automated systems for continuous SpO2 monitoring or oxygen titration relevant to adult LTOT, focusing on accuracy, motion robustness, clinical performance, demographic equity, and readiness for home or ambulatory deployment. This review followed PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 and PRISMA-S (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses-Search). PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Springer Link, ACM Digital Library, and supplementary MDPI publisher-level searches were searched for English-language peer-reviewed studies published during 2000 to January 2025. Eligible studies evaluated AI-driven or automated systems for continuous SpO2 monitoring or oxygen titration in adult LTOT-relevant populations and addressed motion artifact, low-perfusion signal management, skin tone bias, or prolonged signal stability. Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data; disagreements were resolved with a third reviewer. Risk of bias was assessed using an adapted Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) framework. Heterogeneous designs and outcomes precluded meta-analysis, so findings were synthesized narratively following Popay et al. Of 928 records (926 from databases or platforms and 2 from manual reference screening), 912 remained after deduplication, 61 full texts were assessed, and 8 studies were included. Five studies evaluated AI-based systems and 3 evaluated automated non-AI oxygen delivery. AI models reported SpO2 estimation mean absolute error as low as 0.57% and root mean square error as low as 0.69%, but most were simulated, retrospective, or non-chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) specific. Only Cabanas et al reported skin tone-stratified bias analysis. Automated systems showed stronger clinical deployment evidence: O2matic maintained the target SpO2 85.1% of the time versus 46.6% with manual titration, while Cirio and Nava reported mean SpO2 of 95% versus 93% manually. Risk of bias was moderate to serious, mainly due to participant selection, limited demographic reporting, and algorithmic transparency. AI-driven and automated LTOT-relevant systems address complementary gaps. AI approaches show promise for signal interpretation and personalized prediction, whereas rule-based automated systems have stronger near-term clinical evidence for oxygen titration. Evidence is limited by small study numbers, heterogeneous outcomes, limited COPD or home LTOT validation, and sparse equity reporting. Future work should prioritize longitudinal validation in diverse LTOT populations, prespecified equity outcomes, failure-mode reporting, and hybrid architectures combining AI signal intelligence with safety-critical automated control.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning Approaches for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Diagnosis: Protocol for a Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) affects over 366 million adults and 139 million children worldwide, yet diagnosis remains fundamentally subjective, relying on clinical interviews, behavioral observations, and rating scales that yield inconsistent results across practitioners and settings. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) offer a paradigm shift toward objective, data-driven diagnosis by detecting complex patterns across neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and digital biomarkers that elude conventional assessment. Although AI-based ADHD research has grown exponentially, no comprehensive synthesis examines the full spectrum of data modalities, validation practices, and clinical translation readiness. This gap limits our understanding of which approaches are most promising for real-world implementation. This scoping review will visually map the current evidence on AI-based ADHD classification with respect to predictive accuracy, data forms, data features, generalizability, and interpretability of models. This scoping review will use the Joanna Briggs Institute approach to scoping reviews and follow the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. Five electronic databases (IEEE Xplore, Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, and ACM Digital Library) will be systematically searched for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2019 and April 2026. Empirical studies in English involving the use of AI, ML, DL, or explainable AI to diagnose ADHD with a total sample size greater than 100 participants (ADHD and control groups combined) and a non-ADHD control group (individuals with typical development or healthy individuals) will be included. Two independent reviewers will screen the titles, abstracts, and full texts, and any conflicts will be resolved through either discussion or arbitration. A standardized Microsoft Excel template will be used to extract data that will include the following: bibliographic data, data modalities, data models, data validation approaches, performance metrics, and explainability approaches. Thematic and narrative analysis will be used to synthesize findings on 4 research questions that will address model performance, data modality contributions, data characteristics, and interpretability methods. The scoping review began in December 2025. Analysis and screening are in progress, with the scoping review expected to be completed and submitted for publication in June 2026. This scoping review will provide the first comprehensive synthesis of AI-, ML-, and DL-based ADHD diagnostic classification studies, mapping the evidence across data modalities, validation practices, interpretability methods, and clinical translation readiness. Findings will inform future methodological standards and support the translation of AI-based diagnostic tools into clinical practice.

papers.title: [Health care needs comprehensive assessment of caregivers of elderly patients with cognitive disorders].
papers.abstract: Many caregivers provide home care for older adults with cognitive impairment, potentially putting their own health at risk. To assess caregivers' self-reported healthcare needs and identify risk factors for caregiver stress. This cross-sectional study included 133 caregiver-older adult dyads involving older adults with cognitive impairment followed at the Centre Gérontologique Départemental 13 in Marseille, France, in 2023. Caregiver needs were assessed using the interRAI SCaN (Self-Reported Carer Needs) comprehensive assessment tool. High caregiver stress was defined as a desire to reduce or discontinue caregiving. Most caregivers were women, with a mean age of 65 years, and 41.4% had been providing care for more than 5 years. Anxiety was reported by 65%, depression by 59%, sleep disturbances by 72%, and daily pain by 57%. High caregiver stress affected 24% of the sample. In multivariable analysis, high caregiver stress was significantly associated with symptoms of depression (OR = 1.6), difficulties providing care in a timely manner (OR = 2.7), and lack of time for leisure activities (OR = 5.5). Caregivers reported substantial mental health difficulties. Factors associated with caregiver stress were multidimensional, while engagement in social and leisure activities may play a protective role. Early comprehensive assessment of caregivers' healthcare needs and support for maintaining leisure activities may help prevent caregiver burnout.

papers.title: Procrastination among US college students: Prevalence and impact relative to common health and life issues.
papers.abstract: Procrastination is unnecessary delay that can cause various problems. There are uncertainties around how common exactly it is among students, how much it affects them, and how its prevalence and impact compare to those of other issues that students regularly face. Accordingly, this study examines data from 65,950 students (in all degree types and stages), who were surveyed across 97 US institutions of higher education as part of the American College Health Association-National College Health Assessment (ACHA-NCHA). Students were asked about 36 life and health issues, like procrastination, career, finances, appearance, family, bullying, anxiety, depression, ADHD, sleep difficulties, allergies, and influenza. Procrastination was found to be the most common issue that students reported (functionally tied with stress), affecting 72.3% of them. Procrastination was also the issue that most often harmed students' academic performance, affecting 45.4% of them (62.7% of those who experienced it), which was several times as often as issues like finances (2.8x) and ADHD (3.5x). And, procrastination was the most common cause of significant distress compared to the other life issues, affecting 45.7% of students (63.2% of those who experienced it). These rates were higher among undergraduate students, although procrastination was a leading issue among graduate and professional students too. This sheds light on the scale of student procrastination-both in absolute terms and relative to other issues they face-and highlights the need to address it using relevant interventions.

papers.title: Who is disrupting whom? Examining the nighttime activity patterns of humans and their dogs.
papers.abstract: Few studies have examined the nighttime dynamic between humans and dogs, but existing research suggests dogs can disrupt human sleep. In this study, we examined the nighttime activity of 25 Canadian participants, totaling 38 human-dog pairs using accelerometers and survey data. We used linear mixed effects models to assess the drivers of variability in both human sleep and dog nighttime activity, and a generalized linear model to assess the effects of demographic variables on self-reported sleep quality. None of the variables significantly affected objective sleep measures in humans or dog nighttime activity. Dog sleeping location did not affect human perceived sleep quality, but having multiple dogs was associated with poorer subjective sleep (p = 0.042). Human and dog nighttime activities were found to be significantly correlated. Additionally, we conducted a time series analysis to determine lagged correlations between human and dog activities within five minutes. Among the 61% dyads that showed correlation in activity states, human activity preceding dog activity (45%) occurred more often than dog activity preceding human activity (18%). In 36% of dyads, activity was synchronized within the same 1-minute period. Overall, co-sleeping (i.e., bedsharing) had no effect on sleep duration or efficiency in humans or nighttime activity in dogs. The only significant predictor we found was the presence of other dogs, which affected subjective but not objective human sleep quality, revealing a discrepancy between self-reported and objectively measured sleep. Both humans and their dogs impact the nighttime activity of one another, demonstrating our species' inseparable and reciprocal relationship.

papers.title: Dual-Compartment Proteomic analysis reveals inflammatory signatures of sleep disturbance in allergic rhinitis.
papers.abstract: Introduction Allergic rhinitis (AR) is often accompanied by sleep disturbance, while the molecular mechanisms underlying sleep-related exacerbation of nasal symptoms remain poorly understood. This study aimed to investigate the inflammatory protein signatures associated with poor sleep in AR using a dual-compartment proteomic approach. Methods We first analyzed 3,731 adult participants from the 2005-2006 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) cycle to validate the association between sleep duration and AR. We then enrolled 40 AR patients (20 poor sleepers, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index [PSQI] > 5; 20 normal sleepers, PSQI ≤ 5) and performed Olink proteomic profiling in paired serum and nasal secretion (NS) samples. Differential expression analysis, functional enrichment, cross-compartment correlation, Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, and sequential multivariable linear regression were conducted. Results In NHANES, short sleep duration (<6 h) was significantly associated with increased odds ratio (OR) of AR (OR = 1.27, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.05-1.54, P = 0.013) and elevated serum total immunoglobulin E (IgE). In the clinical cohort, poor sleepers had higher Total Nasal Symptom Score (TNSS) (P < 0.001), Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI) (P < 0.001), and blood eosinophil counts (P = 0.011). Proteomics identified 27 serum and 20 NS differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), with 9 overlapping DEPs enriched in interleukin-17 (IL-17), tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and chemokine signaling pathways. A four-marker panel (serum beta-nerve growth factor [β-NGF], serum transforming growth factor-beta 1 [TGF-β1], NS interleukin-8 [IL-8], NS matrix metalloproteinase-1 [MMP-1]) achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.88 (95% CI 0.76-0.97, P < 0.001) for distinguishing poor from normal sleepers. Cross-compartment correlation analysis revealed significant serum-NS protein concordance, consistent with systemic-local inflammatory crosstalk. Sequential multivariable regression showed that serum β-NGF independently predicted TNSS severity even after PSQI adjustment (β = 2.22, P = 0.044), whereas nasal IL-8 was fully attenuated (β = 0.58, P = 0.391). Conclusion Poor sleep is associated with exacerbated AR through coordinated systemic and local inflammatory responses. Serum β-NGF is independently associated with nasal symptoms, whereas the association of NS IL-8 with symptoms appears to be explained by sleep disturbance. Integrating markers from both compartments enhances the identification of AR patients with poor sleep.
